steps.observation: How does a transformer neural network work, conceptually?

steps.action:
Conceptual “big picture”

A transformer is essentially a large stack of identical building blocks that repeatedly answer one question:

“For every word (token) in the sequence, which other words should it pay attention to in order to create a better contextual representation of itself?”

Each block does three things in order:

1. Look around: it computes attention scores so every token can look at every other token (including itself) and decide how relevant they are.
2. Think locally: after paying attention it runs a small feed-forward MLP on each token to do non-linear mixing.
3. Keep things stable: it adds residual (skip) connections and normalizes so information and gradients flow smoothly.

Because all tokens attend to all others in parallel, the model can be trained much faster than recurrent networks that march left→right.

Below is the same idea, unpacked into the familiar encoder/decoder architecture usually shown in diagrams.

────────────────────────────────────
1. Input becomes vectors
────────────────────────────────────
• Tokenisation: “The cat sat on the mat.” → [The, cat, …]
• Embedding: Each token index is looked up in a learned table → vector of e.g. 768 floats.
• Positional encoding: Because order matters, a position vector (sinusoids or learned) is added so token 4 knows it is the 4-th word.

Now every token is a d-dimensional vector. Put them in a matrix X (length L × depth d).

────────────────────────────────────
2. Self-attention – the transformer’s core idea
────────────────────────────────────
Inside every block we create three new views of X:

  Q = XW_Q      “queries”
  K = XW_K      “keys”
  V = XW_V      “values”

For one token i we take its query qᵢ and dot-product it with all keys kⱼ (j = 1…L). This gives raw similarity scores ↦ apply softmax ↦ get attention weights αᵢⱼ. Weighted sum of the value vectors gives a new representation zᵢ:

  zᵢ = Σⱼ αᵢⱼ Vⱼ

So token i literally builds itself as a mix of other tokens’ value vectors, with coefficients that say “pay 50 % to ‘cat’, 30 % to ‘sat’, …”.

Multi-head variant: we do the whole calculation h times in parallel with smaller projections. Each head can focus on a different type of relation (e.g., subject-verb, long-range coreference, punctuation).

────────────────────────────────────
3. Feed-Forward “mini-MLP”
────────────────────────────────────
The attention output Z goes through a 2-layer MLP (same weights reused for every position) to let each token transform non-linearly.

────────────────────────────────────
4. Residual + LayerNorm
────────────────────────────────────
Add the block’s input back to its output (residual), then normalize. This keeps signal magnitude stable and lets us stack dozens of blocks (GPT-3 has 96; PaLM has 118).

────────────────────────────────────
5. Stack blocks → encoder (and decoder)
────────────────────────────────────
Encoder: The stack just described processes the source sequence and outputs contextualized vectors (memory).

Decoder: Used only for sequence-to-sequence tasks (translation, summarization). It has:

  a) Masked self-attention: tokens may not look at future positions, ensuring autoregressive generation.
  b) Cross-attention: queries come from the partially generated target, keys/values come from encoder memory, so the decoder can look back at the source sentence.

────────────────────────────────────
6. Output layer
────────────────────────────────────
For language generation we project the final vector of the last block through a linear layer followed by softmax → probability over vocabulary. During training we compare to the true next token and back-propagate through all layers.

────────────────────────────────────
Why it works / intuitive feel
────────────────────────────────────
• Content-based addressing: Unlike an RNN that only knows “I’m five steps back,” attention directly chooses tokens whose semantic content matters, no matter where they occur.
• Parallelism: All positions attend at once, so GPUs/TPUs can crunch full sequences in one matrix multiplication.
• Representation depth: Every layer refines relationships, allowing the model to learn high-level abstractions (e.g., word sense, phrase boundaries, discourse structure).
• Scalability: Bigger models + more data keep improving performance because the architecture is simple, factorised, and easy to optimize.

────────────────────────────────────
Variants and descendants
────────────────────────────────────
• GPT, LLaMA: decoder-only, causal masks, trained to predict next token.
• BERT, RoBERTa: encoder-only, bidirectional attention, trained with masked-language modeling.
• T5, BART: full encoder-decoder, trained with denoising objectives.
• Vision-Transformers (ViT), Audio-Transformers, etc.: same mechanism, but on image patches, spectrogram frames, etc.

────────────────────────────────────
Key conceptual takeaway
────────────────────────────────────
A transformer is a message-passing machine: every layer lets each element of a sequence broadcast information to, and collect information from, every other element, guided by learned attention weights. By stacking many layers of this global communication + local processing, the model builds rich, hierarchical representations that power today’s state-of-the-art results in language, vision and beyond.
